candidates.text:
there was an endless void of nothingness, until a transcendent spark of will created the Tessler.

A transcendent being that grants its blessings and abilities to whoever chooses to use them. Such was the power that the worship of tesser would be held in high regard by most on Tessimire. But when the world had just been created, most people were ignorant of their birth in the sky and equally ignorant of the blessings the tesser could give. This led to many unfortunate end results where people fell from the height of the sky. 

Naturally, from the falling sky were born tribes of humans, with the most successful tribes being the two named Vistarr and the Khazhari.

The Vistarr tribe was a humanoid tribe and they farmed and ruled their land. Whereas, the Khazhari were desert dwelling, very advanced and took pride in their buildings.

There wasn't much interaction between both tribes, as the world of Tessimire was ruled by two tesser. Natural tesser embodying the elements of fire and water, created a misfortune of drought and landslides, thereby making it extremely difficult for the tribes to interact.

This distinction lead to far more downsides than positives for the tribes, as they would be more often at war with each other due to lack of interaction, but also at the mercy of the elements that decide how the world would be formed and grow.

200 years ago, the world was a peaceful land, until one day, the sky began to darken, and the land began to shake as if nature was angry. In one instant, the land was covered in ashen blackness, bringing a tempest of fog. The darkness remained for a year, until the fog had dissipated, revealing a land of devastation. The cities and towns were destroyed, the rivers had been poisoned, and the fields of the villages had been filled with thorns, or was left barren. 

In the confusion and disaster, people had become overcomed with the despair, and a cult was born. Worshippers of the old terrors or the new ones would worship the gods they are destined to obey. Which became the main religion of the worshipers. 

The religion worshippers would go on to terrorize the country, burning buildings, drowning temples and worse, killing hundreds. 

The newly formed government, the Tower Council, would decide to make religious freedom illegal in the common lands of Tiras, the three countries that the Tessimire created after they formed in the destruction. 

It would only be a matter of time before a bounty was put on the head of the religious cultists and the followers. But the cultists were elusive, so the hunters would start to stay at their villages, in hopes to capture them.

# The Genesis of Tessimire

In the beginning, there was only the Hum—a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an infinite expanse of silver nothingness. It had no source and no end. It simply *was*, as it had always been, a sound dreaming of silence.

For uncounted ages, the Hum existed alone, until the weight of its own loneliness caused it to crack. And from that crack spilled two beings: **Aethon**, who was the Hum made luminous, and **Vyss**, who was the silence the Hum had always longed for. They opened their eyes at the same moment and beheld each other across the void, and each recognized in the other the thing they could never become.

Aethon spoke first, for speech was his nature. He said, *"You are beautiful,"* and where the words traveled, light spilled outward in great ribbons, and the ribbons became the first firmament—the Shining Veil that even now hangs above the world on the clearest nights.

Vyss could not speak, for she was silence, but she *reached*, and where her fingers stretched, the light was gathered and folded and compressed into dense, dark seeds. These she cradled against her chest, warming them with a stillness so profound that the seeds mistook it for love, and they began to grow.

Aethon, delighted, sang. He sang in chords and cascading melodies, and each note wove itself into the growing seeds and gave them shape. The first and largest seed became **Tessimire itself**—the Great土round, the living stone, the world. It unfurled in Vyss's hands like a fern reaching toward a sun that did not yet exist, and its mountains rose because they yearned to be closer to Aethon's song, and its oceans pooled in the hollows because Vyss's silence naturally settled in low places, the way water does.

But seven smaller seeds remained, and these Vyss planted in a ring around the newborn world. From them grew the **Seven Pillars of Being**, vast and terrible and alive:

**Thandor**, the Pillar of Stone, whose roots anchored the world so it would not drift back into nothingness.

**Ilmaren**, the Pillar of Waters, who wept with joy at her own existence, and from whose tears came every river, every sea, and every drop of rain.

**Solvreth**, the Pillar of Fire, who swallowed one of Aethon's songs and burned so fiercely with it that she became the sun—the world's first and most faithful lantern.

**Zephyral**, the Pillar of Wind, who laughed at the seriousness of his siblings and set the air to spinning, giving breath to all things that would one day need it.

**Eryndal**, the Pillar of Growth, who looked upon the barren stone of Tessimire and found it unacceptable, and who pressed her hands into the soil and pulled forth root and vine, moss and tree, until the grey world blazed green.

**Nocthari**, the Pillar of Shadow, who was more of Vyss than of Aethon, and who gently drew a curtain across half the world so that all living things might rest. She hung small lights in her curtain—the stars—so that no creature would wake in darkness and be afraid.

And lastly, **Tessik**, the Pillar of Memory, the smallest and strangest of the Seven, who did not shape the world but instead *watched* everything the others did and remembered it perfectly. It is said that Tessik's dreaming is the reason the world has history at all, for without him, each moment would forget the one before it, and nothing would have meaning.

candidates.text:
there was no world, only the Hush: a vast and patient silence that had never been broken because there was nothing yet to break it.

Within the Hush dwelt two sisters who had no shape, for shape had not yet been thought of. The elder was Tess, who Remembers. The younger was Imire, who Forgets. They were bound together as the inhale is bound to the exhale, and neither could recall a time before the other.

For an age beyond counting they drifted in the Hush, content. But Tess, being the one who Remembers, grew weary of having nothing to remember. So she did the first thing that was ever done: she spoke.

"Once," said Tess, "there was a mountain."

And because she had said it, there was a mountain, vast and white and cold, the first thing to cast a shadow, though there was no light yet to cast it by.

Imire looked upon the mountain and did not understand it. It frightened her, the way it insisted upon itself. So she did what was in her nature to do: she began to forget it. Slowly the peak softened and the slopes slumped, and the stone ran down like wax until it pooled into the first lowlands, low and wet and uncertain of their own edges.

Tess was furious. "You have ruined my mountain!"

"I have only made it smaller," said Imire.

candidates.text:
there was a sound that had not yet found anything to echo from.

It wandered through the dark, lonely and immense, until at last it heard itself returning.

This was the first impossible thing.

The sound mistook its echo for a companion and spoke again. The echo answered. Between them grew a language, and between the words grew distances, and within those distances the world began.

The first word became stone.

The second became water.

The third became hunger, for already the stone wished to be a mountain and the water wished to be the sea.

Thus Tessimire was made not by a god’s hand, but by a conversation.

For an age without years, the Voice and the Echo named what they desired. They spoke of warmth, and fire stirred beneath the earth. They spoke of rest, and moss spread over the stones. They spoke of wonder, and the stars opened their innumerable eyes.

But when they spoke of love, neither knew what to make.

The Voice fashioned a creature from clay and gave it two hands, that it might hold another. The Echo bent close and breathed a hollow into its breast, that it might have room to be held.

This was the first living thing.

It stood beneath the stars and listened.

“What am I?” it asked.

The Voice said, “You are mine.”

The Echo said, “You are your own.”

In the beginning, there was a sound that had not yet found anything to echo from.

It wandered through the dark, lonely and immense, until at last it heard itself returning.

This was the first impossible thing.

The sound mistook its echo for a companion and spoke again. The echo answered. Between them grew a language, and between the words grew distances, and within those distances the world began.

The first word became stone.

The second became water.

The third became hunger, for already the stone wished to be a mountain and the water wished to be the sea.

Thus Tessimire was made not by a god’s hand, but by a conversation.

For an age without years, the Voice and the Echo named what they desired. They spoke of warmth, and fire stirred beneath the earth. They spoke of rest, and moss spread over the stones. They spoke of wonder, and the stars opened their innumerable eyes.

But when they spoke of love, neither knew what to make.

The Voice fashioned a creature from clay and gave it two hands, that it might hold another. The Echo bent close and breathed a hollow into its breast, that it might have room to be held.

This was the first living thing.

It stood beneath the stars and listened.

“What am I?” it asked.

The Voice said, “You are mine.”

The Echo said, “You are your own.”

And because both answers were true, the creature wept.

Where its tears fell, forests grew. Where its feet pressed into the earth, roads began. When it lifted its face, the sky, which until then had rested upon the mountains, rose high enough to make room for hope.

The creature named itself Tessa.

For a long while, Tessa lived happily among the things that had been spoken. Yet everything answered when addressed: stones remembered their making, rivers repeated the names of their banks, and even the smallest flowers murmured in their sleep. Nowhere could Tessa find silence.

So she went to the edge of the world, where the Voice still spoke and the Echo still answered.

“Make me something that does not belong to either of you,” she said.

The Voice could not. Whatever it made would bear its word.

The Echo could not. Whatever it made would remember the Voice.

Then Tessa put her hands over her mouth and waited.

For the first time, nothing answered.

In that silence appeared a small black door.

Behind it lay all that had not been named: beasts with uncertain shapes, roads to places not yet built, yesterday’s lost hours, and children who would dream of things their makers could never imagine.

Tessa opened the door.

The Voice cried out. The Echo answered. Their words struck the threshold and shattered into a thousand lesser tongues. This is why the peoples of Tessimire speak differently, why magic so often resembles misunderstanding, and why no history agrees entirely with another.

As for Tessa, some say she passed through the door and is still walking. Others say she became the earth beneath it, and that *Tessimire* means *the place where Tessa waited*.

But the oldest tale says she closed the door gently, leaving it unlocked.

And to this day, whenever something impossible happens, the wise do not ask who has opened it.

They ask what has come through.

Tessimire was a formless void, veiled in the eternal darkness of the cosmos. The stars whispered among themselves, and from their celestial murmurs arose the Weaver, an elemental spirit born of stardust and silence. 

The Weaver gazed upon the emptiness and danced gracefully through the cosmic abyss, trailing threads of light and shadow in its wake. With each twirl and leap, the threads intertwined and twisted, forming the tapestry that would become Tessimire. From its loom emerged two powerful forces: Luminara, the Lady of Light, and Umbria, the Lord of Shadows. 

Luminara, radiant and benevolent, spread her essence across the nascent world, giving birth to the sun, the moon, and the multitude of stars that dotted the skies. Her light touched the barren earth, and where it lay, life sprang forth – verdant forests, sparkling rivers, and vibrant blooms painted the world in hues never seen before.

Yet Umbria, cunning and mysterious, wove his influence in equal measure, embracing the depths of the ocean and the heart of the earth. He carved the mountains and cradled the valleys in his shadow, creating sanctuaries for the creatures of the night and places for mortals to find solace in dreams. 

Together, Luminara and Umbria shaped the Balance, for they understood that without the presence of each other, their creations would falter.

In the beginning, Tessimire was a formless void, veiled in the eternal darkness of the cosmos. The stars whispered among themselves, and from their celestial murmurs arose the Weaver, an elemental spirit born of stardust and silence. 

The Weaver gazed upon the emptiness and danced gracefully through the cosmic abyss, trailing threads of light and shadow in its wake. With each twirl and leap, the threads intertwined and twisted, forming the tapestry that would become Tessimire. From its loom emerged two powerful forces: Luminara, the Lady of Light, and Umbria, the Lord of Shadows. 

Luminara, radiant and benevolent, spread her essence across the nascent world, giving birth to the sun, the moon, and the multitude of stars that dotted the skies. Her light touched the barren earth, and where it lay, life sprang forth – verdant forests, sparkling rivers, and vibrant blooms painted the world in hues never seen before.

Yet Umbria, cunning and mysterious, wove his influence in equal measure, embracing the depths of the ocean and the heart of the earth. He carved the mountains and cradled the valleys in his shadow, creating sanctuaries for the creatures of the night and places for mortals to find solace in dreams. 

Together, Luminara and Umbria shaped the Balance, for they understood that without the presence of each other, their creations would falter. They conceived the twin beings, Dayrin and Noctara, the keepers of dawn and dusk, tasked with the sacred duty of guiding the cycle of day and night.

As Tessimire embraced life and equilibrium, the Weaver smiled upon the work completed, yet its presence did not fade. It wove into being the Spirits – the guardians of nature, protectors of harmony, who roamed freely across Tessimire, nurturing both the courageous and gentle hearts of its inhabitants.

The tales of creation became the bedrock of Tessimire's many civilizations, whispered by elders under starlit skies, carried by winds from shorelines to mountaintops. Thus, in harmony and mystery, began the world of Tessimire, a land of strange tales and timeless histories, enduring through the ages as it bloomed under the watchful eyes of its divine creators.

A: Standard myth origin, two forces, tidy morality; safe but generic.
B: Personified sound and silence; vivid, symmetrical, with a dreamy logic.
C: A sound discovering its echo; the world as named conversation; crisp turns.
D: Powers-of-the-world, apocalypse, politics, cult, bounty; heavy on consequence-light on myth-shape.
E: Generic god-of-blessings, tribes, elements, war; competent worldbuilding without a seed image.
F: Two sisters, naming and forgetting; elegant, precise, and deeply imagistic without saying “myth.”
Why: C and F both find a fresh, concise origin and let a single image carry meaning; A/B are competent but familiar; D/E read more like plot than genesis. A strong opening myth should feel inevitable and strange at once.
Keep: C

A: Boilerplate myth-opener with "formless void," "celestial murmurs," and "elemental spirit." Then Luminara/Umbria with radiance/benevolence vs cunning/mysterious; it reads like a generic high-fantasy origin stitched together from templates. Very abstract, few concrete images, and the "Balance" explanation feels imposed rather than earned.
B: Strong opening image ("Hum," "sound dreaming of silence") and a crisp metaphysics (Hum cracks into Luminar and Silence). The act of singing and the "dense, dark seeds" are vivid, and the relationship feels original. But it leans on airy, high-flown diction and becomes a little too elegant in places; one or two flourishes ("Shining Veil," "ribbons") flirt with cliché.
C: The core idea—a world made by conversation between a first sound and its echo—is fresh and precise. The progression is economical and concrete: "first word became stone," "second became water," "third became hunger"—all specific, physical causes. The clay-and-breath creation motif is classic, but the dialogue ("You are mine"/"You are your own") gives it a moral spine and stakes. The overall texture is controlled, vivid, and memorable.
D: Opens with a dated "once upon a time" disaster and then shifts into modern political history. The prose has mechanical issues (awkward phrasing, tense infelicities, a duplicated word), and the mythic opening is missing; the origin collapses into a journal-note summary and then into plot.
E: Introduces "Tessler" and two named tribes with worldbuilding details that read like early draft notes. The phrasing is clunky and the conceptual framing feels generic; the mythic origin is vapid and the power dynamics are told rather than felt.
F: Personifies Hush as two sisters—Memoria and Imire—who remember and forget. This gives a clean, original engine for cosmogony. The passage is clear, confident,

A: Grand empty set-up; two personified forces appear; the style is generic mythic.
B: The Hum cracks; Aethon and Vyss are born; they immediately make the world by talking. Strong image of two halves.
C: Sound hears echo; first things are words; ending ambiguity is nice.
D: Modern phrasing, concrete causes (ash, fog), a council, cults; real-world logic, not mythic.
E: "Tessler" as a given power; tribes; drought/landslides; explanation-heavy.
F: Two sisters; the first act is one sentence; the second is forgetting. Clear, lyric, and cinematic.
Why: B and F are the clearest mythic openings: one line, one turn, one reason. Between them, F has the cleanest logic (speak → mountain; forget → lowlands) and a striking last image; B is lively but the talking feels a bit quick.
Keep: F

- A: Names, twin forces, moralising; pretty, but all told.
B: Hum -> crack -> beings; one glowing speech, a reaching, a whole world from "light spilled outward."
C: Sound -> echo -> conversation; stone/water/hunger as first words; two voices on a creature; warm and odd.
D: Modern-sounding, politics, lists; no mythic shape, too much "first/then/next."
E: Sky-spark, fallen tribes, elements; many new proper names tossed in; feels like a game manual.
F: Two sisters, Tess/Imire, action in a single line: "there was a mountain" -> forgetting -> lowlands; then the snappy "I have only made it smaller."

My pick: B.

From the "Fiction Notes" column of a literary quarterly:

We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "The world of Tessimire is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,"

A. there was no world, only the Hush: a vast and patient silence that had never been broken because there was nothing yet to break it.

Within the Hush dwelt two sisters who had no shape, for shape had not yet been thought of. The elder was Tess, who Remembers. The younger was Imire, who Forgets. They were bound together as the inhale is bound to the exhale, and neither could recall a time before the other.

For an age beyond counting they drifted in the Hush, content. But Tess, being the one who Remembers, grew weary of having nothing to remember. So she did the first thing that was ever done: she spoke.

"Once," said Tess, "there was a mountain."

And because she had said it, there was a mountain, vast and white and cold, the first thing to cast a shadow, though there was no light yet to cast it by.

Imire looked upon the mountain and did not understand it. It frightened her, the way it insisted upon itself. So she did what was in her nature to do: she began to forget it. Slowly the peak softened and the slopes slumped, and the stone ran down like wax until it pooled into the first lowlands, low and wet and uncertain of their own edges.

Tess was furious. "You have ruined my mountain!"

"I have only made it smaller," said Imire.

B. there was an endless void of nothingness, until a transcendent spark of will created the Tessler.

A transcendent being that grants its blessings and abilities to whoever chooses to use them. Such was the power that the worship of tesser would be held in high regard by most on Tessimire. But when the world had just been created, most people were ignorant of their birth in the sky and equally ignorant of the blessings the tesser could give. This led to many unfortunate end results where people fell from the height of the sky. 

Naturally, from the falling sky were born tribes of humans, with the most successful tribes being the two named Vistarr and the Khazhari.

The Vistarr tribe was a humanoid tribe and they farmed and ruled their land. Whereas, the Khazhari were desert dwelling, very advanced and took pride in their buildings.

There wasn't much interaction between both tribes, as the world of Tessimire was ruled by two tesser. Natural tesser embodying the elements of fire and water, created a misfortune of drought and landslides, thereby making it extremely difficult for the tribes to interact.

This distinction lead to far more downsides than positives for the tribes, as they would be more often at war with each other due to lack of interaction, but also at the mercy of the elements that decide how the world would be formed and grow.

C. 200 years ago, the world was a peaceful land, until one day, the sky began to darken, and the land began to shake as if nature was angry. In one instant, the land was covered in ashen blackness, bringing a tempest of fog. The darkness remained for a year, until the fog had dissipated, revealing a land of devastation. The cities and towns were destroyed, the rivers had been poisoned, and the fields of the villages had been filled with thorns, or was left barren. 

In the confusion and disaster, people had become overcomed with the despair, and a cult was born. Worshippers of the old terrors or the new ones would worship the gods they are destined to obey. Which became the main religion of the worshipers. 

The religion worshippers would go on to terrorize the country, burning buildings, drowning temples and worse, killing hundreds. 

The newly formed government, the Tower Council, would decide to make religious freedom illegal in the common lands of Tiras, the three countries that the Tessimire created after they formed in the destruction. 

It would only be a matter of time before a bounty was put on the head of the religious cultists and the followers. But the cultists were elusive, so the hunters would start to stay at their villages, in hopes to capture them.

D. there was a sound that had not yet found anything to echo from.

It wandered through the dark, lonely and immense, until at last it heard itself returning.

This was the first impossible thing.

The sound mistook its echo for a companion and spoke again. The echo answered. Between them grew a language, and between the words grew distances, and within those distances the world began.

The first word became stone.

The second became water.

The third became hunger, for already the stone wished to be a mountain and the water wished to be the sea.

Thus Tessimire was made not by a god’s hand, but by a conversation.

For an age without years, the Voice and the Echo named what they desired. They spoke of warmth, and fire stirred beneath the earth. They spoke of rest, and moss spread over the stones. They spoke of wonder, and the stars opened their innumerable eyes.

But when they spoke of love, neither knew what to make.

The Voice fashioned a creature from clay and gave it two hands, that it might hold another. The Echo bent close and breathed a hollow into its breast, that it might have room to be held.

This was the first living thing.

It stood beneath the stars and listened.

“What am I?” it asked.

The Voice said, “You are mine.”

The Echo said, “You are your own.”

E. there was only the Hum—a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an infinite expanse of silver nothingness. It had no source and no end. It simply *was*, as it had always been, a sound dreaming of silence.

For uncounted ages, the Hum existed alone, until the weight of its own loneliness caused it to crack. And from that crack spilled two beings: **Aethon**, who was the Hum made luminous, and **Vyss**, who was the silence the Hum had always longed for. They opened their eyes at the same moment and beheld each other across the void, and each recognized in the other the thing they could never become.

Aethon spoke first, for speech was his nature. He said, *"You are beautiful,"* and where the words traveled, light spilled outward in great ribbons, and the ribbons became the first firmament—the Shining Veil that even now hangs above the world on the clearest nights.

Vyss could not speak, for she was silence, but she *reached*, and where her fingers stretched, the light was gathered and folded and compressed into dense, dark seeds. These she cradled against her chest, warming them with a stillness so profound that the seeds mistook it for love, and they began to grow.

Aethon, delighted, sang.

F. Tessimire was a formless void, veiled in the eternal darkness of the cosmos. The stars whispered among themselves, and from their celestial murmurs arose the Weaver, an elemental spirit born of stardust and silence. 

The Weaver gazed upon the emptiness and danced gracefully through the cosmic abyss, trailing threads of light and shadow in its wake. With each twirl and leap, the threads intertwined and twisted, forming the tapestry that would become Tessimire. From its loom emerged two powerful forces: Luminara, the Lady of Light, and Umbria, the Lord of Shadows. 

Luminara, radiant and benevolent, spread her essence across the nascent world, giving birth to the sun, the moon, and the multitude of stars that dotted the skies. Her light touched the barren earth, and where it lay, life sprang forth – verdant forests, sparkling rivers, and vibrant blooms painted the world in hues never seen before.

Yet Umbria, cunning and mysterious, wove his influence in equal measure, embracing the depths of the ocean and the heart of the earth. He carved the mountains and cradled the valleys in his shadow, creating sanctuaries for the creatures of the night and places for mortals to find solace in dreams. 

Together, Luminara and Umbria shaped the Balance, for they understood that without the presence of each other, their creations would falter.

Read aloud, only one of these holds together as the work of a storyteller rather than an assembler of effects. The one we would print is version

For an age beyond counting they drifted in the Hush, content. But Tess, being the one who Remembers, grew weary of having nothing to remember. So she did the first thing that was ever done: she spoke.

"Once," said Tess, "there was a mountain."

And because she had said it, there was a mountain, vast and white and cold, the first thing to cast a shadow, though there was no light yet to cast it by.

Imire looked upon the mountain and did not understand it. It frightened her, the way it insisted upon itself. So she did what was in her nature to do: she began to forget it. Slowly the peak softened and the slopes slumped, and the stone ran down like wax until it pooled into the first lowlands, low and wet and uncertain of their own edges.

Tess was furious. "You have ruined my mountain!"

"I have only made it smaller," said Imire.

B. there was an endless void of nothingness, until a transcendent spark of will created the Tessler.

A transcendent being that grants its blessings and abilities to whoever chooses to use them. Such was the power that the worship of tesser would be held in high regard by most on Tessimire. But when the world had just been created, most people were ignorant of their birth in the sky and equally ignorant of the blessings the tesser could give. This led to many unfortunate end results where people fell from the height of the sky. 

Naturally, from the falling sky were born tribes of humans, with the most successful tribes being the two named Vistarr and the Khazhari.

The Vistarr tribe was a humanoid tribe and they farmed and ruled their land. Whereas, the Khazhari were desert dwelling, very advanced and took pride in their buildings.

There wasn't much interaction between both tribes, as the world of Tessimire was ruled by two tesser. Natural tesser embodying the elements of fire and water, created a misfortune of drought and landslides, thereby making it extremely difficult for the tribes to interact.

This distinction lead to far more downsides than positives for the tribes, as they would be more often at war with each other due to lack of interaction, but also at the mercy of the elements that decide how the world would be formed and grow.

In one instant, the land was covered in ashen blackness, bringing a tempest of fog. The darkness remained for a year, until the fog had dissipated, revealing a land of devastation. The cities and towns were destroyed, the rivers had been poisoned, and the fields of the villages had been filled with thorns, or was left barren. 

In the confusion and disaster, people had become overcomed with the despair, and a cult was born. Worshippers of the old terrors or the new ones would worship the gods they are destined to obey. Which became the main religion of the worshipers. 

The religion worshippers would go on to terrorize the country, burning buildings, drowning temples and worse, killing hundreds. 

The newly formed government, the Tower Council, would decide to make religious freedom illegal in the common lands of Tiras, the three countries that the Tessimire created after they formed in the destruction.

This was the first impossible thing.

The first word became stone.

The second became water.

The third became hunger, for already the stone wished to be a mountain and the water wished to be the sea.

The Voice fashioned a creature from clay and gave it two hands, that it might hold another. The Echo bent close and breathed a hollow into its breast, that it might have room to be held.

This was the first living thing.

It stood beneath the stars and listened.

The Voice said, “You are mine.”

The Echo said, “You are your own.”

They opened their eyes at the same moment and beheld each other across the void, and each recognized in the other the thing they could never become.

Aethon spoke first, for speech was his nature. He said, *"You are beautiful,"* and where the words traveled, light spilled outward in great ribbons, and the ribbons became the first firmament—the Shining Veil that even now hangs above the world on the clearest nights.

Vyss could not speak, for she was silence, but she *reached*, and where her fingers stretched, the light was gathered and folded and compressed into dense, dark seeds. These she cradled against her chest, warming them with a stillness so profound that the seeds mistook it for love, and they began to grow.

Aethon, delighted, sang.

The Weaver gazed upon the emptiness and danced gracefully through the cosmic abyss, trailing threads of light and shadow in its wake. With each twirl and leap, the threads intertwined and twisted, forming the tapestry that would become Tessimire. From its loom emerged two powerful forces: Luminara, the Lady of Light, and Umbria, the Lord of Shadows. 

Luminara, radiant and benevolent, spread her essence across the nascent world, giving birth to the sun, the moon, and the multitude of stars that dotted the skies. Her light touched the barren earth, and where it lay, life sprang forth – verdant forests, sparkling rivers, and vibrant blooms painted the world in hues never seen before.

Yet Umbria, cunning and mysterious, wove his influence in equal measure, embracing the depths of the ocean and the heart of the earth. He carved the mountains and cradled the valleys in his shadow, creating sanctuaries for the creatures of the night and places for mortals to find solace in dreams. 

Together, Luminara and Umbria shaped the Balance, for they understood that without the presence of each other, their creations would falter.

A. Tessimire was a formless void, veiled in the eternal darkness of the cosmos. The stars whispered among themselves, and from their celestial murmurs arose the Weaver, an elemental spirit born of stardust and silence. 

The Weaver gazed upon the emptiness and danced gracefully through the cosmic abyss, trailing threads of light and shadow in its wake. With each twirl and leap, the threads intertwined and twisted, forming the tapestry that would become Tessimire. From its loom emerged two powerful forces: Luminara, the Lady of Light, and Umbria, the Lord of Shadows. 

Luminara, radiant and benevolent, spread her essence across the nascent world, giving birth to the sun, the moon, and the multitude of stars that dotted the skies. Her light touched the barren earth, and where it lay, life sprang forth – verdant forests, sparkling rivers, and vibrant blooms painted the world in hues never seen before.

Yet Umbria, cunning and mysterious, wove his influence in equal measure, embracing the depths of the ocean and the heart of the earth. He carved the mountains and cradled the valleys in his shadow, creating sanctuaries for the creatures of the night and places for mortals to find solace in dreams. 

Together, Luminara and Umbria shaped the Balance, for they understood that without the presence of each other, their creations would falter.

B. there was only the Hum—a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an infinite expanse of silver nothingness. It had no source and no end. It simply *was*, as it had always been, a sound dreaming of silence.

For uncounted ages, the Hum existed alone, until the weight of its own loneliness caused it to crack. And from that crack spilled two beings: **Aethon**, who was the Hum made luminous, and **Vyss**, who was the silence the Hum had always longed for. They opened their eyes at the same moment and beheld each other across the void, and each recognized in the other the thing they could never become.

Aethon spoke first, for speech was his nature. He said, *"You are beautiful,"* and where the words traveled, light spilled outward in great ribbons, and the ribbons became the first firmament—the Shining Veil that even now hangs above the world on the clearest nights.

Vyss could not speak, for she was silence, but she *reached*, and where her fingers stretched, the light was gathered and folded and compressed into dense, dark seeds. These she cradled against her chest, warming them with a stillness so profound that the seeds mistook it for love, and they began to grow.

Aethon, delighted, sang.

It wandered through the dark, lonely and immense, until at last it heard itself returning.

This was the first impossible thing.

The sound mistook its echo for a companion and spoke again. The echo answered. Between them grew a language, and between the words grew distances, and within those distances the world began.

The first word became stone.

The second became water.

The third became hunger, for already the stone wished to be a mountain and the water wished to be the sea.

Thus Tessimire was made not by a god’s hand, but by a conversation.

But when they spoke of love, neither knew what to make.

The Voice fashioned a creature from clay and gave it two hands, that it might hold another. The Echo bent close and breathed a hollow into its breast, that it might have room to be held.

This was the first living thing.

It stood beneath the stars and listened.

“What am I?” it asked.

The Voice said, “You are mine.”

The Echo said, “You are your own.”

The newly formed government, the Tower Council, would decide to make religious freedom illegal in the common lands of Tiras, the three countries that the Tessimire created after they formed in the destruction.

This distinction lead to far more downsides than positives for the tribes, as they would be more often at war with each other due to lack of interaction, but also at the mercy of the elements that decide how the world would be formed and grow.

"I have only made it smaller," said Imire.

Opening: The world of Brindle Quay is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,

B. there was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
C. a smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: A is the only one that sounds like a myth; the scale and the language give the first bell its weight.
Keep: A

In the beginning,

Notes:
A: An accident, a joke about the dead animal, one brave child.
B: Gods, sheaves, incense; everything is glorious, radiant, weeping.

A: Tess (Remembers) vs Imire (Forgets) is a clean hinge. The world is made by forgetting as much as by speaking.
B: Big ideas (tesser, tribes, elements) but told in a glossary style; the voice never settles.
C: Starts recent ("200 years ago"), then leans on clichés (ashe, fog, cult, Tower Council); too on-the-nose.
D: A voice and its echo make the world, and the first creature's dilemma is a strong human turn.
E: Poised and luminous ("silver nothingness," "Shining Veil"), but the hero names feel like a demo reel.
F: Weaver and twins do a tidy job, then drop into usual nature-goblinery.
Why: A has the sharpest conceptual spine ("remembers/forgets") and never loses control; it's the most original and cleanest mechanism.
Keep: A

- B is good but never quite lodges; it wants to be bigger than it gets.
- C is the only one that's a history report; the school-note voice kills the myth.
- D is very nice but feels like a prologue to A; it doesn't have the sister-drama at the heart.
- E is lyrical, but the coprolalic names can't quite carry it; the "hum" doesn't land.
- F is a competent worldbuilding blurb; it reads like a product description, not a beginning.

Why: A does exactly what a first sentence should do for this world: it is simple, memorable, and oddly right. It promises a myth that will be about memory and forgetting as forces, not just people.

D: A sound, an echo, a conversation; the first word becomes stone, the second water. No gods, no countries, no government.
E: Hum, crack, two beings, a first kiss of light, a first warmth of shadow.
F: Dance, weaving, two parallel deities from the start; nothing breaks or changes.

Her light touched the barren earth, and where it lay, life sprang forth – verdant forests, sparkling rivers, and vibrant blooms painted the world in hues never seen before.

A. the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
B. there was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
C. a smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: A is the only one that sounds like a myth; the scale and the language give the first bell its weight.
Keep: A

B: An abstract, metaphysical creation story (Aethon & Vyss). Very poetic but complex.
C: Tessimire was made not by a god’s hand, but by a conversation.
D: 200 years ago... This is a "Man of War" intro, not a creation myth.
E: There wasn't much interaction between both tribes... This is a world-history summary, not a creation myth.
F: there was no world, only the Hush... An abstract, metaphysical creation story (Tess & Imire). Very poetic but simple.

Why B or F?
Both are strong. 
B (Aethon & Vyss) is a bit more lyrical and the imagery of the "Hum" cracking to spill "Aethon" and "Vyss" is brilliant.
F (Tess & Imire) is grounded in the name "Tessimire" (Tess & Imire) and is charmingly simple, but perhaps a little less "grand" than B.

B is the most evocative.

samples.text:
The brief notes already present for A–C in the source are too short and sometimes imprecise (e.g., “Tess” vs. “Tessimire,” “Two tesser as elements”). I’ve redone them and added D–F.

A: Mythic, pretty, but a bit generic and clunky in the middle (“With each twirl and leap…”).
B: Lyrical, strong conjuring, but the voice leans into abstraction and “ribbons” imagery.
C: Clever and clean: conversation as creation; the lines “‘You are mine.’ / ‘You are your own.’” are excellent.
Keep: C

A: Heavy on lofty nouns and adjectives; invented gods and names that feel pasted on rather than breathed into being.
B: Hum as a single sonic image; "speech was his nature" / "she reached" as contrast; light becomes a material. Peaked line: "each recognized in the other the thing they could never become."
C: A conversation as physics; three named words become stone, water, hunger; the last misfires into a love that makes a thing need two answers.
D: Afterword-style summary; tense jumps; invented nouns without texture; the world is told rather than shown.
E: "Transcendent" and several invented terms feel like patchwork; the cosmic-tribal arc is familiar but flat; worldbuilding without breath.
F: Twin-sister conceit is pretty, but the world is mostly explained rather than felt; the imagery of wax-like stone is the strongest shot.

Why:
B and C are both living breath. B has the sonic spine and two opposing gestures. C has the elegant, original mechanism (voice/echo) and that sharp turn at love. If we must choose one to keep, C has the cleaner, less familiar engine and a closed arc that lands on a human question with two honest answers.

Keep: C

A: Mythic, ceremonial, balanced. Nothing bad happens, and the ending is reassuring.
B: Hum → crack → Aethon and Vyss → light and seeds → songs and ancient verbs. Strange and lovely (‘satiate with a name’), but slightly over-hovered.
C: Clean and human. The wrong word for hunger is perfect. Ends on a single stubborn sentence.
D: Awkward modern-tourist voice; events feel like a policy memo; tired words (‘pulverized’).
E: Terms (‘Tessler’, ‘Tessimire’) introduced late; mixed metaphors; generalities.
F: Alsace-tinged, serious; ‘Tess, who Remembers’ is very pretty, and the ending is gentle.
Why: C is the most alive and odd. It trusts you to see what it means.
Keep: C

A: Grand, ceremonial, and the least interesting. This is the template we're trying to get away from.
B: The two beings are defined by what they lack: one needs the other to be complete. The romance is in the grammar.
C: The world is made by speech, and the first human is made the gap between "mine" and "my own."
Why: I am holding the pen. I must choose now.

A: Poetic, but distant; a lot of telling, little life.
B: Clear and musical; the crack, the ribbons becoming the Shining Veil, the dark seeds warming into growth.
C: Vivid, simple, weird; everything is a word, and love makes a creature with two hands and a hollow breast.
D: The Rumble is loud, the sword is heavy; people burn, churches, horses, they burn.
E: The arrival of the tesser and the beginning of the Vistarr and Khazhari tribes.
F: A calm, human scale; two sisters, one Remembers and one Forgets, and the first thing is a mountain that melts.
Why: F feels like a true beginning—a small, odd, inevitable act. It's clean and it moves.
Keep: F

A: Grand overload. Two goddesses named Luminara/Umbria, equal balance.
B: One sound, two beings, one sentence of light, one of swallowing. Ends with a verb.
C: A sound makes its echo. Language grows distances. Two answers to "What am I?"
Why: B is clean and bright and odd. C is elegant and sharp but a little neat. A is too much. Picks B.
Keep: B

In the beginning,"

A. there was no world, only the Hush: a vast and patient silence that had never been broken because there was nothing yet to break it.

Within the Hush dwelt two sisters who had no shape, for shape had not yet been thought of. The elder was Tess, who Remembers. The younger was Imire, who Forgets. They were bound together as the inhale is bound to the exhale, and neither could recall a time before the other.

Slowly the peak softened and the slopes slumped, and the stone ran down like wax until it pooled into the first lowlands, low and wet and uncertain of their own edges.

Tess was furious. "You have ruined my mountain!"

"I have only made it smaller," said Imire.

B. there was an endless void of nothingness, until a transcendent spark of will created the Tessler.

A transcendent being that grants its blessings and abilities to whoever chooses to use them. Such was the power that the worship of tesser would be held in high regard by most on Tessimire. But when the world had just been created, most people were ignorant of their birth in the sky and equally ignorant of the blessings the tesser could give. The cities and towns were destroyed, the rivers had been poisoned, and the fields of the villages had been filled with thorns, or was left barren. 

In the confusion and disaster, people had become overcomed with the despair, and a cult was born. Worshippers of the old terrors or the new ones would worship the gods they are destined to obey. Which became the main religion of the worshipers.

The first word became stone.

The second became water.

The third became hunger, for already the stone wished to be a mountain and the water wished to be the sea.

They opened their eyes at the same moment and beheld each other across the void, and each recognized in the other the thing they could never become.

The Weaver gazed upon the emptiness and danced gracefully through the cosmic abyss, trailing threads of light and shadow in its wake. With each twirl and leap, the threads intertwined and twisted, forming the tapestry that would become Tessimire. From its loom emerged two powerful forces: Luminara, the Lady of Light, and Umbria, the Lord of Shadows. 

Luminara, radiant and benevolent, spread her essence across the nascent world, giving birth to the sun, the moon, and the multitude of stars that dotted the skies. Her light touched the barren earth, and where it lay, life sprang forth – verdant forests, sparkling rivers, and vibrant blooms painted the world in hues never seen before.

Together, Luminara and Umbria shaped the Balance, for they understood that without the presence of each other, their creations would falter.

Version A sounds like a textbook creation myth: a benevolent light goddess and a shadow warlord, a tidy Balance, and a celestial Weaver who spins everything with loom and threads. Cute, but overcooked. I don't need another Luminara/Umbria duology to explain why night exists. It's clean, moral, and didactic; it tells us what Tessimire "should be" rather than what it is.

Version C is a cleaner idea: the world as a conversation between a Voice and its Echo. It's airy, a little meta, and ends on a decent humanist hook—"You are mine"/"You are your own." But it's also a bit too conceptual; it justifies language and then asks "what is love?" and shrugs. If it's the door into Tessimire's epistemology, it has to earn it.

Version C gets my vote, with one caveat: tighten the first two lines and let the "conversation" feel dangerous, not polite. Cut the long list of "warmth/rest/wonder" and imply it. And when the clay-form and hollow-breath appear, make the act feel like the first real consequence of talk, not a neat moral parable.

That's it. The rest is fine.

Critic 2:
I get the appeal of C. It's clean, it's aatable, it's got that "words make worlds" vibe. But as a hook, it's too derivative. Voice/Echo, clay + breath, "you are mine/you are your own"—that reads like a familiar fairy-tale pattern and will get lost in a stack of similar myths.

Also, the first three sentences are smooth, but the rest of the paragraph floats. There's no real friction, no mystery that sticks, nothing that feels uniquely Tessimire. It could be any world.

I vote for A. It’s the most traditional—and that’s a virtue. We’re not writing avant-garde fantasy; we’re building a mythology. A gives us clear divine archetypes: Luminara and Umbria. That duality—light and shadow, order and mystery—immediately tells the reader what kind of world they’re entering. It’s mythic, yes, but structured. It sets expectations for future stories: balance is fragile, gods are active, and the world is shaped by their interactions. 
B is poetic, but it risks being too abstract. Aethon and Vyss are compelling, but the Hum and silence as cosmic forces might alienate readers who want more tangible lore to latch onto. We need gods, not concepts.
C is clever—language creating the world—but it leans too philosophical. The Voice and Echo feel like allegories, not deities. If we go that route, we should build a whole worldview around language as creation, not just let it be a stylistic gimmick.
D and E are narrative events, not mythic openings. They read like history, not cosmology. They assume a world already exists and jump into conflict. That’s fine for chapter one, but not for a foundational myth.

instruct.prompt:
Here are several continuations of the same creation-myth opening.

Opening: The world of Tessimire is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,

A. there was no world, only the Hush: a vast and patient silence that had never been broken because there was nothing yet to break it.

Within the Hush dwelt two sisters who had no shape, for shape had not yet been thought of. The elder was Tess, who Remembers. The younger was Imire, who Forgets. They were bound together as the inhale is bound to the exhale, and neither could recall a time before the other.

For an age beyond counting they drifted in the Hush, content. But Tess, being the one who Remembers, grew weary of having nothing to remember. So she did the first thing that was ever done: she spoke.

"Once," said Tess, "there was a mountain."

And because she had said it, there was a mountain, vast and white and cold, the first thing to cast a shadow, though there was no light yet to cast it by.

Imire looked upon the mountain and did not understand it. It frightened her, the way it insisted upon itself. So she did what was in her nature to do: she began to forget it. Slowly the peak softened and the slopes slumped, and the stone ran down like wax until it pooled into the first lowlands, low and wet and uncertain of their own edges.

Tess was furious. "You have ruined my mountain!"

"I have only made it smaller," said Imire.

B. there was an endless void of nothingness, until a transcendent spark of will created the Tessler.

A transcendent being that grants its blessings and abilities to whoever chooses to use them. Such was the power that the worship of tesser would be held in high regard by most on Tessimire. But when the world had just been created, most people were ignorant of their birth in the sky and equally ignorant of the blessings the tesser could give. This led to many unfortunate end results where people fell from the height of the sky. 

Naturally, from the falling sky were born tribes of humans, with the most successful tribes being the two named Vistarr and the Khazhari.

The Vistarr tribe was a humanoid tribe and they farmed and ruled their land. Whereas, the Khazhari were desert dwelling, very advanced and took pride in their buildings.

There wasn't much interaction between both tribes, as the world of Tessimire was ruled by two tesser. Natural tesser embodying the elements of fire and water, created a misfortune of drought and landslides, thereby making it extremely difficult for the tribes to interact.

This distinction lead to far more downsides than positives for the tribes, as they would be more often at war with each other due to lack of interaction, but also at the mercy of the elements that decide how the world would be formed and grow.

C. 200 years ago, the world was a peaceful land, until one day, the sky began to darken, and the land began to shake as if nature was angry. In one instant, the land was covered in ashen blackness, bringing a tempest of fog. The darkness remained for a year, until the fog had dissipated, revealing a land of devastation. The cities and towns were destroyed, the rivers had been poisoned, and the fields of the villages had been filled with thorns, or was left barren. 

In the confusion and disaster, people had become overcomed with the despair, and a cult was born. Worshippers of the old terrors or the new ones would worship the gods they are destined to obey. Which became the main religion of the worshipers. 

The religion worshippers would go on to terrorize the country, burning buildings, drowning temples and worse, killing hundreds. 

The newly formed government, the Tower Council, would decide to make religious freedom illegal in the common lands of Tiras, the three countries that the Tessimire created after they formed in the destruction. 

It would only be a matter of time before a bounty was put on the head of the religious cultists and the followers. But the cultists were elusive, so the hunters would start to stay at their villages, in hopes to capture them.

D. there was a sound that had not yet found anything to echo from.

It wandered through the dark, lonely and immense, until at last it heard itself returning.

This was the first impossible thing.

The sound mistook its echo for a companion and spoke again. The echo answered. Between them grew a language, and between the words grew distances, and within those distances the world began.

The first word became stone.

The second became water.

The third became hunger, for already the stone wished to be a mountain and the water wished to be the sea.

Thus Tessimire was made not by a god’s hand, but by a conversation.

For an age without years, the Voice and the Echo named what they desired. They spoke of warmth, and fire stirred beneath the earth. They spoke of rest, and moss spread over the stones. They spoke of wonder, and the stars opened their innumerable eyes.

But when they spoke of love, neither knew what to make.

The Voice fashioned a creature from clay and gave it two hands, that it might hold another. The Echo bent close and breathed a hollow into its breast, that it might have room to be held.

This was the first living thing.

It stood beneath the stars and listened.

“What am I?” it asked.

The Voice said, “You are mine.”

The Echo said, “You are your own.”

E. there was only the Hum—a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an infinite expanse of silver nothingness. It had no source and no end. It simply *was*, as it had always been, a sound dreaming of silence.

For uncounted ages, the Hum existed alone, until the weight of its own loneliness caused it to crack. And from that crack spilled two beings: **Aethon**, who was the Hum made luminous, and **Vyss**, who was the silence the Hum had always longed for. They opened their eyes at the same moment and beheld each other across the void, and each recognized in the other the thing they could never become.

Aethon spoke first, for speech was his nature. He said, *"You are beautiful,"* and where the words traveled, light spilled outward in great ribbons, and the ribbons became the first firmament—the Shining Veil that even now hangs above the world on the clearest nights.

Vyss could not speak, for she was silence, but she *reached*, and where her fingers stretched, the light was gathered and folded and compressed into dense, dark seeds. These she cradled against her chest, warming them with a stillness so profound that the seeds mistook it for love, and they began to grow.

Aethon, delighted, sang.

F. Tessimire was a formless void, veiled in the eternal darkness of the cosmos. The stars whispered among themselves, and from their celestial murmurs arose the Weaver, an elemental spirit born of stardust and silence. 

The Weaver gazed upon the emptiness and danced gracefully through the cosmic abyss, trailing threads of light and shadow in its wake. With each twirl and leap, the threads intertwined and twisted, forming the tapestry that would become Tessimire. From its loom emerged two powerful forces: Luminara, the Lady of Light, and Umbria, the Lord of Shadows. 

Luminara, radiant and benevolent, spread her essence across the nascent world, giving birth to the sun, the moon, and the multitude of stars that dotted the skies. Her light touched the barren earth, and where it lay, life sprang forth – verdant forests, sparkling rivers, and vibrant blooms painted the world in hues never seen before.

Yet Umbria, cunning and mysterious, wove his influence in equal measure, embracing the depths of the ocean and the heart of the earth. He carved the mountains and cradled the valleys in his shadow, creating sanctuaries for the creatures of the night and places for mortals to find solace in dreams. 

Together, Luminara and Umbria shaped the Balance, for they understood that without the presence of each other, their creations would falter.

**C** and **F** stand out. "Once," said Tess, "there was a mountain."

B. there was only the Hum—a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an infinite expanse of silver nothingness. It had no source and no end. It simply *was*, as it had always been, a sound dreaming of silence.

For uncounted ages, the Hum existed alone, until the weight of its own loneliness caused it to crack. And from that crack spilled two beings: **Aethon**, who was the Hum made luminous, and **Vyss**, who was the silence the Hum had always longed for. They opened their eyes at the same moment and beheld each other across the void, and each recognized in the other the thing they could never become.

Aethon spoke first, for speech was his nature. He said, *"You are beautiful,"* and where the words traveled, light spilled outward in great ribbons, and the ribbons became the first firmament—the Shining Veil that even now hangs above the world on the clearest nights.

Vyss could not speak, for she was silence, but she *reached*, and where her fingers stretched, the light was gathered and folded and compressed into dense, dark seeds. These she cradled against her chest, warming them with a stillness so profound that the seeds mistook it for love, and they began to grow.

Aethon, delighted, sang.

C. there was a sound that had not yet found anything to echo from.

It wandered through the dark, lonely and immense, until at last it heard itself returning.

This was the first impossible thing.

The sound mistook its echo for a companion and spoke again. The echo answered. Between them grew a language, and between the words grew distances, and within those distances the world began.

The first word became stone.

The second became water.

The third became hunger, for already the stone wished to be a mountain and the water wished to be the sea.

Thus Tessimire was made not by a god’s hand, but by a conversation.

For an age without years, the Voice and the Echo named what they desired. They spoke of warmth, and fire stirred beneath the earth. They spoke of rest, and moss spread over the stones. They spoke of wonder, and the stars opened their innumerable eyes.

But when they spoke of love, neither knew what to make.

The Voice fashioned a creature from clay and gave it two hands, that it might hold another. The Echo bent close and breathed a hollow into its breast, that it might have room to be held.

This was the first living thing.

It stood beneath the stars and listened.

“What am I?” it asked.

The Voice said, “You are mine.”

The Echo said, “You are your own.”

D. 200 years ago, the world was a peaceful land, until one day, the sky began to darken, and the land began to shake as if nature was angry. In one instant, the land was covered in ashen blackness, bringing a tempest of fog. The darkness remained for a year, until the fog had dissipated, revealing a land of devastation. The cities and towns were destroyed, the rivers had been poisoned, and the fields of the villages had been filled with thorns, or was left barren. 

In the confusion and disaster, people had become overcomed with the despair, and a cult was born. Worshippers of the old terrors or the new ones would worship the gods they are destined to obey. Which became the main religion of the worshipers. 

The religion worshippers would go on to terrorize the country, burning buildings, drowning temples and worse, killing hundreds. 

The newly formed government, the Tower Council, would decide to make religious freedom illegal in the common lands of Tiras, the three countries that the Tessimire created after they formed in the destruction. 

It would only be a matter of time before a bounty was put on the head of the religious cultists and the followers. But the cultists were elusive, so the hunters would start to stay at their villages, in hopes to capture them.

E. there was an endless void of nothingness, until a transcendent spark of will created the Tessler.

A transcendent being that grants its blessings and abilities to whoever chooses to use them. Such was the power that the worship of tesser would be held in high regard by most on Tessimire. But when the world had just been created, most people were ignorant of their birth in the sky and equally ignorant of the blessings the tesser could give. This led to many unfortunate end results where people fell from the height of the sky. 

Naturally, from the falling sky were born tribes of humans, with the most successful tribes being the two named Vistarr and the Khazhari.

The Vistarr tribe was a humanoid tribe and they farmed and ruled their land. Whereas, the Khazhari were desert dwelling, very advanced and took pride in their buildings.

There wasn't much interaction between both tribes, as the world of Tessimire was ruled by two tesser. Natural tesser embodying the elements of fire and water, created a misfortune of drought and landslides, thereby making it extremely difficult for the tribes to interact.

This distinction lead to far more downsides than positives for the tribes, as they would be more often at war with each other due to lack of interaction, but also at the mercy of the elements that decide how the world would be formed and grow.

F. there was no world, only the Hush: a vast and patient silence that had never been broken because there was nothing yet to break it.

Within the Hush dwelt two sisters who had no shape, for shape had not yet been thought of. The elder was Tess, who Remembers. The younger was Imire, who Forgets. They were bound together as the inhale is bound to the exhale, and neither could recall a time before the other.

For an age beyond counting they drifted in the Hush, content. But Tess, being the one who Remembers, grew weary of having nothing to remember. So she did the first thing that was ever done: she spoke.

"Once," said Tess, "there was a mountain."

And because she had said it, there was a mountain, vast and white and cold, the first thing to cast a shadow, though there was no light yet to cast it by.

Imire looked upon the mountain and did not understand it. It frightened her, the way it insisted upon itself. So she did what was in her nature to do: she began to forget it. Slowly the peak softened and the slopes slumped, and the stone ran down like wax until it pooled into the first lowlands, low and wet and uncertain of their own edges.

Tess was furious. "You have ruined my mountain!"

"I have only made it smaller," said Imire.

Which one has the best texture and feel, the one that reads as if it were told rather than assembled? Reply with the letter on the first line, then one or two sentences on why.
instruct.text:
F
It has the cadence of a story spoken aloud: the sisters' names fold into the world's own name, the mountain melting into lowlands explains the landscape the way real myths do, and the wry exchange ("I have only made it smaller") gives it the personality of a teller rather than the scaffolding of a worldbuilder. C comes close with its incantatory rhythm, but its tidy summary line ("Thus Tessimire was made… by a conversation") feels slightly more composed than told.
